summary: Block. npm test passes 120/120, npm run check 11/11 and tests/bash-prose.test.mjs 13/13. Attempt 4's whole-call rule closes every write-then-run spelling from a1 to a3. A probe of HEAD against the working tree, confirmed in real bash 3.2 and zsh 5.9, finds two single-call bypasses that HEAD denied. (F-1) Under an unquoted delimiter, bash joins backslash-newline in the body before it looks for the terminator. A body line `E\` followed by `OF` therefore ends the heredoc in bash, but not in the guard, so the guard drops the next line as body: a reset, a force push to main or a secrets read after it is allowed and runs. This breaks C-1. (F-2) The push rule and the push deny pattern now stop at a raw newline. A push whose line leaves `$(`, a backtick or a quote open carries main or --force onto the next line, and bash passes that word to the same git push. HEAD denied this; it is now allowed in building and done. This breaks the guards spec rule that the default branch is never pushed. Loop diagnosis: the builder's fault, not the critics' or the spec's. The a1-a3 critic findings were real regressions, and each attempt fixed what was named. The a4 critic passed without probing terminator parsing or multi-line pushes, and its one major finding (write in one call, run in a later one) is overturned as F-3: C-1 mandates it, and the Write tool already allowed it at HEAD. The criteria are sound: C-3 holds if a line means a shell line, as the builder already does for backslash-newline. Both fixes are small and fail safe, so no human hold is needed.

findings.issue: Under an unquoted delimiter, bash removes backslash-newline from the body before matching the terminator, but dropFileHeredocs matches raw lines and checks only for `$` and backtick. A body `E\` then `OF` ends the heredoc in bash, yet the guard drops the following command line as body, so a reset, force push or secrets read after it is allowed and runs in the same call.
findings.suggestion: Under an unquoted delimiter, keep the text whole when any body line ends in a backslash (or contains one), and add the A1-A4 probe shapes to tests/bash-prose.test.mjs as denied.

dropFileHeredocs output for A1: "cat > notes.md <<EOF\nEOF" (the reset line is gone)

findings.issue: The push rule (`[^|;&\n]*`) and the push deny pattern in profiles/default.json line 63 stop at a raw newline, but bash continues a command across a newline inside `$(`, a backtick or a quote. `git push origin goal/G-3 $(` / `echo main` / `)` pushes main, and the same shape with `--force` force-pushes; HEAD denied both, the working tree allows them in building and in done.
findings.suggestion: When the push line leaves a quote, `$(`, `(` or a backtick open, judge the push through to the end of the text (or deny it); keep the newline boundary only for a balanced line, and add the B1-B5 shapes to the push test as denied.

Real bash with a git stub: B1-shape: git-arg[push] git-arg[origin] git-arg[goal/G-3] git-arg[main]; B4-shape: ... git-arg[main]; B5-shape: ... git-arg[--push-option=a\nb] git-arg[main] (zsh identical)

findings.issue: Overturns the attempt-4 critic's major finding F-1 (a heredoc writes a denied command to a file and a later call runs it). C-1 requires dropping a file-writing body, and the same content can already be written by the Write tool, whose guard never sees the content, so the gap was open at HEAD and is not a regression of this slice. The sharpest form, a heredoc that writes .git/hooks/pre-commit, is worth a follow-up goal, not a block here.

evidence.quote: Write tool to .git/hooks/pre-commit (content never judged, pre-existing path): allow
A cat or tee heredoc body that writes a denied command to a file is allowed in its own call, and a later call that runs the file is also allowed

findings.issue: The push rule compares raw words, so a one-line `git push origin goal/G-3 'main'` or `git push origin goal/G-3 $(echo main)` pushes main and is allowed; HEAD allowed both too.
findings.suggestion: Strip quotes from push arguments and treat an argument with `$(`, a backtick or `$` as unknown, which fails safe; a separate goal.
